**My reasoning, as this farmer:**

I've been working this land in Quzhou for over fifty years. My body isn't what it was — I can't do the heavy hand-digging anymore — so I hire someone with a rotary tiller and a harvester. That's how everyone does it now. My son is in the city. I manage about 5 mu on my own.

There's no question what I'll plant. Wheat in winter, maize in summer. Same as last year, same as thirty years ago. That's the rotation here. The soil suits it, the water suits it, and I know it. I'm not going to try cotton or vegetables at my age — that's too much labor and too much uncertainty.

For wheat, I use the seed the village committee distributes — it's a certified variety, gives reliable yield, and I don't have to worry about it. For maize, I buy hybrid seed from the supply store in town. Hybrid maize is what everyone buys now; it yields more and I've seen that myself.

For fertilizer I put down compound fertilizer at planting time, then top-dress with urea when the wheat joints and again when the maize is waist-high. I know people say I use too much, but I'm not going to risk a thin harvest to save on fertilizer. It's the yield that matters.

Wheat needs water three times — before winter freeze-in, at jointing, and at heading. Maize I'll water once or twice depending on the rains in July and August. If it's a wet summer I might not water at all.

I'll spray herbicide on the wheat after it emerges, and then fungicide twice in spring to keep the rust and powdery mildew off — those are the things that cut my yield if I ignore them. For maize, I spray herbicide right after planting and watch for corn borers in late July.

I plant maize straight into the wheat stubble with no extra tillage. The machine can handle it, and it saves me time and money.
